column6: YHWH says his name is for ever and his memorial through all generations; this makes the divine name itself an enduring object of remembrance beside 87:1 and 87:15.
The Hebrew זִכְרִי (“my memorial”) is from זכר, cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label; here God's name is the memorial kept across generations.
YHWH says he will come and bless wherever he causes his name to be remembered; the Hebrew אזכיר uses זכר, cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label, in a worship setting.
God promises presence and blessing at the altar where his name is remembered; this ties remembrance of the name to embodied worship.

column5: Elijah's spoken prayer at the offering
column6: At the evening offering Elijah addresses YHWH by name and asks that Israel know he is God; this is a public, voiced prayer embedded in ritual worship.
Elijah asks YHWH to hear so the people will know him and their hearts will turn back; this joins invocation, response, and inward return in a single prayer.

column5: reading followed by confession and worship
column6: The community spends one part of the day reading the Torah and another confessing and worshiping YHWH; this concretely joins recitation and prayer in one service.
The speaker thanks God with the whole heart and glorifies his name forever; this joins inward intention and praise of the name.

column5: glory due the name and an offering
column6: Worshipers ascribe YHWH glory due his name and bring an offering into his courts; this places name-praise and ritual action together.
The Hebrew calls for thanks to God's holy memorial, using זכר, cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label; remembrance here is voiced praise.

column5: Hebrew זכר, praise at God's memorial
column6: The verse joins singing to YHWH with giving thanks at the memorial of his holiness; its זכר noun is cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label.

column5: Hebrew זכר and the enduring name
column6: The verse says YHWH's name and memorial endure through generations; זכר is cognate with the commentary's ذ ك ر label, and directly couples name with remembrance.
The psalm places YHWH's enduring name beside his memorial through all generations; this gives a scriptural counterpart to remembering the Lord's name.
One generation is to praise God's works to the next and declare his mighty acts; this is a specific form of recitation and reminder.
The psalm ends with the speaker's mouth praising YHWH and all flesh blessing his holy name forever; this joins tongue and name-praise.
The worshiper ascribes glory due YHWH's name, brings an offering, and bows in holy array; this is a specific conjunction of praise and bodily ritual.

column5: Aramaic צלי, prayer for the king
column6: The Aramaic form מְצַלַּיִן means “they pray” for the king and his sons; it is a close Semitic counterpart to the commentary's ص ل و label, though the etymological relation to Arabic ṣalāt is uncertain.
The decree asks that temple offerings be made to heaven's God and prayers offered for the king; this places bodily cult and supplication together.
After the fire and glory appear, Israel bows face to the ground and worships; this gives a specific bodily response after prayer and offering.
The speaker is warned not to rush words or heart in prayer before God; this adds a concrete caution about outward speech and inward attention to the commentary's account of vocal and hidden worship.

column5: lips honoring while the heart is distant
column6: Isaiah condemns people whose lips honor God while their hearts are far away; this sharpens the distinction between spoken devotion and inward reality that the commentary develops through loud and hidden.
Jesus quotes Isaiah's lips-honor/heart-distant charge against people who worship in vain; this Christian reading makes inward intention a test of outward religious practice.
When Zechariah's mouth opens and his tongue is freed, he speaks blessing to God; this gives a concrete scene of the tongue becoming an instrument of praise.
Jesus repeatedly withdraws to deserted places to pray; this is a specific secluded form of the prayer whose hidden dimension God knows in 87:7.
Before raising Lazarus, Jesus looks upward and thanks the Father; this is audible prayer in a public scene.
Jesus explains that he spoke for the surrounding crowd to believe; this qualifies the warning against performative prayer by showing an aloud prayer directed to others' understanding.
Stephen calls on the Lord Jesus as he entrusts his spirit to him; this is a specific invocation of the Lord's name within prayer.

column5: kneeling and crying loudly in prayer
column6: Stephen kneels and cries with a loud voice for his killers' forgiveness; this joins bodily posture, audible prayer, and supplication.

column5: teaching and prayers in the community
column6: The first believers devote themselves to apostolic teaching and to prayers; this places recitation/admonition and prayer in the same communal practice.

column5: praying and singing with spirit and mind
column6: Paul says he will pray and sing both with spirit and with mind; this concretely unites verbal prayer, praise, and inward intention.

column5: an audible blessing needs an intelligible Amen
column6: Paul asks how an outsider can say Amen to a blessing if he does not know what was said; this makes the public, voiced character of liturgical prayer explicit.
The elders hold incense bowls that are the prayers of the saints; this gives a Christian vision the same concrete prayer-as-incense image as the psalmic prayer tradition.
The community is told to persist in prayer, watchful with thanksgiving; this is a specific pairing of supplication and praise.

column5: prayer in suffering, praise in joy
column6: James directs the suffering person to pray and the cheerful person to sing praise; this shows prayer and praise as closely related responses within lived practice.
Paul's short command to pray continually makes devotion an ongoing practice, alongside the commentary's recurring remembrance.
The next command is to give thanks in everything; this makes thanksgiving an explicit companion to continual prayer.

column5: thanksgiving for the holy name dwelling in hearts
column6: The eucharistic prayer thanks the Father for his holy name dwelling in believers' hearts; this joins prayer, gratitude, God's name, and inward remembrance.

column5: Kaddish's sanctification of the great name
column6: The Talmud's synagogue response asks that God's great name be blessed; this rabbinic liturgical formula makes praise of the name a communal prayer.
The Mishnah sets times for morning, afternoon, and evening prayer; this gives a concrete Jewish schedule for repeated prayer as a regular practice.

column5: thanksgiving made known to the living
column6: Raphael tells Tobit and Tobias to bless God and make God's goodness known among the living; this is a specific verbal enactment of praise and remembrance.
The verse tells the soul to bless YHWH and not forget his benefits; this is a distinct remembrance claim supporting the commentary's link between worship and avoiding forgetfulness.
The Pharisee thanks God while boasting of his own righteousness; this gives a specific case where prayer's words do not express the inward devotion emphasized by the commentary.
The tax collector stands at a distance, will not lift his eyes, beats his breast, and asks God for mercy; this joins bodily posture and prayer with inward humility.

Jesus says the tax collector, rather than the Pharisee, goes home justified; this makes the quality of the person praying matter, like the commentary's distinction between successful devotion and negligent prayer.
